cim: Five policy planks to prepare U.S. workers for dislocation caused by artificial intelligence
kihagyva: P3: 41 pont, tendencia 20%, jóváhagyás után fordul
cim_eredeti: Five policy planks to prepare U.S. workers for dislocation caused by artificial intelligence
szoveg_eredeti:
The rise of artificial intelligence and the potential for new technology to spark widespread job dislocation reflects a unique challenge for policymakers because of how wide the range of scenarios might be for the depth, breadth and speed of displacement. Economists and technologists have suggested possibilities that range from a transition that is challenging for a subset of workers but in line with prior technological advances to much more dramatic disruptions that dislocate tens of millions of workers, end career paths that previously felt reliable and even lead to a net reduction of jobs with gains concentrated among a relative few.

Our report argues that under almost any scenario, the United States will need a major expansion of worker adjustment policies and that efforts to build those policies should begin now, even as the outlook remains highly uncertain. The United States lags far behind peer nations in having the basic infrastructure today to help support workers who face the potential of AI-induced job dislocation as they transition into new, successful career paths.

Too often, U.S. policymakers and analysts have misinterpreted the well-documented shortfalls of the U.S. workforce training system at large as proof that any type of job training program cannot work. Instead, these shortfalls are often a reflection of the failures of policymakers to invest sufficiently in workforce development systems that employ approaches that have shown evidence of success at a smaller scale, from career counseling to data-driven training programs. We believe that there is an opportunity both to build on past approaches that have been too limited and to develop new models that can help workers recover from painful layoffs. The correct agenda will include expanded transition assistance and wage insurance alongside more novel efforts to prevent layoffs altogether.

This paper argues that making displaced workers universally eligible for these programs, while investing more in training tailored to the unique challenges that AI presents, offers the best roadmap forward. It acknowledges that getting our approach right will require experimentation, both due to past challenges in scaling up programs that have shown initial success and because AI-related displacement may affect new and different segments of the workforce. But in enacting these ideas as a downpayment, policymakers can address the anxiety that is already being felt by many workers and provide them with greater agency in shaping their own futures, all while building workforce institutions that can evolve further as AI’s impact becomes clearer.

We present these ideas with a recognition that any worker transition agenda must be seen as only one element of the policy response that will be needed to address AI’s effects on the labor market. It should go without saying that absent a commitment to ensuring good, available jobs and strong labor markets, no worker adjustment policies can succeed. Any scenario of economic disruption will require policy responses that are both multi-faceted and broad-based, addressing the need to create new jobs, share the gains of AI-induced productivity growth, promote greater worker bargaining power, and protect against workplace abuses. The benefits of job training, for example, will inevitably be limited if there are not good jobs for people to train for, so we also need policies that help create good jobs in scenarios where AI results in a net loss of jobs. At the same time, policies explicitly designed to help workers transition from one job to another will be necessary alongside these other approaches.

Indeed, even the mere possibility of swift, widespread displacement should create the impetus for responsible federal policymakers to invest in an evidence-based approach that is broad enough and capable enough of being scaled up quickly if more dire scenarios come to pass. Given these uncertainties, any approach will require some degree of experimentation and ongoing refinement, recognizing that full answers to the effects of AI on U.S. jobs remain unclear. But that means work at the federal and state level should start now, rather than waiting until more significant disruptions occur, ensuring that there is an infrastructure for transition support that can be expanded as needed.

At the same time, the policies we offer have the virtue of providing much needed support for displaced workers today—even before any major new dislocation has occurred—and for workers in the future who lose their jobs for reasons that extend beyond AI. Indeed, workers and the economy at large might have fared better during the past decades of deindustrialization, the Great Recession of 2007–2009, and the COVID pandemic of 2020–2023 had more robust measures in the areas we describe below been in place.

This report aims to advance these policy discussions by stressing five fundamental approaches that should underpin a worker adjustment package, while offering key program details designed to jumpstart efforts to enact policies now. The policies we describe would build on top of the existing workforce system, filling gaps and experimenting with innovative measures. We believe they should be funded through provisions that would better tax capital and corporate profits, which can ensure that those who benefit from AI-related productivity gains pay for measures to help those who might be displaced.

Below, we briefly describe each of these five principles and how they can be incorporated into a worker adjustment package, before discussing all of them in greater detail in the main body of this report.

While concerns about dislocation have led many economists and policymakers to argue for a strategy that targets those workers who are specifically harmed by AI, history suggests that would be a mistake. Past efforts to target assistance based on the particularcauses of job loss for workers harmed by trade, for example, often fell woefully short, and not simply because they led to inequities for workers suffering similar dislocation for different reasons. Experience shows how difficult it is to make the right causal determinations as to why displaced workers lost their jobs, which can delay or even block aid even to the workers programs are specifically targeted for.

In that light, we propose two major universal job supports, both of which are designed to give all displaced workers the ability to chart their own paths in a changing economy—universal worker adjustment assistance and universal job-search assistance. Like the other proposals we offer in this paper, these new policies should build on top of and complement the existing workforce system, helping to fill gaps that have long left job-seeking workers without sufficient support.

Building off the Trade Adjustment Assistance model—but addressing the flaws that led to it shutting out many of the workers who needed it—we propose a universal worker adjustment assistance program that covers the cost for any displaced worker to pursue training, along with financial assistance to allow workers to afford their basic costs while out of the workforce. The program would provide new funding for workers to receive up to 104 weeks of additional unemployment insurance payments while they participated in training.

Trade Adjustment Assistance provided real benefits to those who received financial support and training under the program, but it ended up excluding many of those it was intended to serve. For example, during a period in the early 2000s when researchers have estimated 2 million workers were dislocated by imports from China, TAA only provided training to fewer than 50,000 workers per year.
